title: Ambrose and the emperor
hookLine: after a massacre, Bishop Ambrose makes Emperor Theodosius do public penance
last: THE LORD, THE GIVER OF LIFE.

lines: A CITY PUNISHED BY ITS EMPEROR.
A BISHOP WHO HAS TO DECIDE.
cards: A city has just been punished by its own emperor. In Thessalonica, after a riot, Emperor Theodosius orders a reprisal, and soldiers kill the people gathered in the city's circus.
The old historians say the guilty and the innocent died together. The emperor is a baptized Christian. His bishop in Milan, Ambrose, has known him well.
Now Ambrose has to decide what a bishop does when a man with that much power has blood on his hands.

teach.h: A PRIVATE LETTER, IN HIS OWN HAND.
teach.b: Two kinds of evidence tell it differently. The first is a letter from Ambrose himself, careful, almost tender. He wrote it in his own hand, he says, so the emperor alone would read it.
He cannot offer the sacrifice of the altar with the emperor present, not until he repents. And he reminds him of King David.
David also sinned terribly, and the prophet Nathan told him a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb.
David burned with anger at the rich man, until Nathan said, in the King James words, "Thou art the man." David confessed. A king who repents, Ambrose says, is not made smaller by it.
The second account is a scene, from the historian Theodoret.

teach.h: A SCENE AT THE CHURCH DOOR.
teach.b: The emperor arrives at the church in Milan, and Ambrose meets him at the door and won't let him in. Theodosius says that David sinned too. Ambrose answers: you followed him in sinning, now follow him in repenting.

Readers handle Theodoret's drama with care; the letter is quieter. But the sources agree on what came next. The emperor did public penance before the people, and only then was received back to communion.

teach.h: ROYAL SIGNS SET ASIDE IN CHURCH.
teach.b: At his funeral, Ambrose recalled it: Theodosius took off the signs of his royalty and wept for his sin in church. Days ago on this path, an emperor's favor turned the church from hunted to favored.
Here is the edge of that favor. Ambrose was no rebel, but he would not pretend. He wrote alone first, and left a door open.
Some see the church standing over the throne; others, a conscience standing before a ruler. Both start from Nathan's line.

how: Christians remember Ambrose as a saint and a bishop of Milan; the story of Theodosius' penance is retold as an example of repentance and of a pastor's courage before power.

o: an emperor who ordered the massacre at Thessalonica
a historian who wrote the scene at the church door
a bishop of Milan who called an emperor to repent

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: tells the scene at the church door

s: Ambrose's first word to the emperor was a public rebuke
his own letter was private, written in his own hand for the emperor alone.
Theodosius set aside the signs of his royalty to repent
Ambrose said so at the emperor's funeral: he wept for his sin in church.
Ambrose's letter and Theodoret tell the story the same way
Theodoret tells a dramatic scene at the church door; Ambrose's letter is quieter. they agree on the penance.

games.q: you're Ambrose. the emperor, a friend of the church, has ordered a massacre. what do you do?
o: say nothing: he protects the church.
write to him privately, and hold back communion until he repents.
denounce him to the crowd before you say a word to him.
games.why: Ambrose wrote alone first, reminding him of David. the penance became public, but the first word was private, and it left a door open.

practice: Let one person with power over others come to mind, someone whose choice troubles you.

If anger comes, set it beside you, and ask what Ambrose seems to have asked: what would a true word sound like, said privately, with a door left open? Just find the sentence, and if you pray, hold that person before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Ambrose. The bishop who said no to an emperor, first in a letter, until the ruler set aside the signs of his royalty to repent. That ends a week of a pilgrim, monks, a city of mercy, a poet, a teacher, and a creed.

orig.note: Greek: repentance, a change of mind. the New Testament word for turning around.

carryVoice: Your line: no one is above it. Not even an emperor on his throne. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ambrose, On the Death of Theodosius 34
